title: Wildfire Technology Is Advancing. Can Organizations Act on the Information Fast Enough?
summary: Wildfire detection technology is advancing fast. Learn why rapid, coordinated communication is what turns early warning into resilience.
body_markdown:
Wildfire detection technology is advancing. Artificial intelligence, drones, predictive modeling, satellite monitoring, and faster data sharing can help agencies identify threats earlier and plan evacuations with greater precision.


But early warning only matters if organizations can turn that intelligence into coordinated action. The central challenge is the same across regions: reaching, coordinating, and mobilizing the right people before conditions change.


Recent fire seasons show why this is an international operational priority. Australia’s


[2019–20 season burned more than 21 million hectares of forest.](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/abares/forestsaustralia/forest-data-maps-and-tools/data-by-topic/fire)


Canada experienced its most destructive season on record in 2023, with


[17.6 million hectares burned.](https://cwfis.cfs.nrcan.gc.ca/en/fire-history)


Southern Europe faced similar pressure, with more than 500,000 hectares burned in 2023. The


[Alexandroupolis fire in Greece alone burned more than 96,000 hectares](https://joint-research-centre.ec.europa.eu/jrc-news-and-updates/wildfires-2023-among-worst-eu-century-2024-04-10_en)


.


The landscapes and reporting methods differ, but the operational challenge is the same: turning early intelligence into coordinated action before a fast-moving fire overwhelms response systems.


Better sensors and models alone do not automatically produce better outcomes.


Earlier detection creates a window of opportunity. Communication determines whether organizations can act on it.


## Every Minute Matters in Wildfire Response


Recent emergencies show how quickly fires can overwhelm manual coordination. Canada’s 2023 season forced an estimated 232,000 people to evacuate during 282 events, according to


[Statistics Canada](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/36-28-0001/2025006/article/00004-eng.htm)


. In southern Europe, the 2023 Alexandroupolis fire became the largest single wildfire recorded in Europe, while Australia’s Black Summer fires crossed jurisdictions and placed sustained pressure on emergency services, utilities, transport networks, healthcare providers, and local authorities.


Events of this scale do not wait for phone trees, email chains, or manual call-down lists. Response decisions often involve several organizations at once: national and local authorities, fire services, utilities, transport operators, schools, healthcare systems, and private-sector partners. Each group needs timely information, but not always the same information or through the same channel.


In that environment, delay becomes risk. A utility operator that learns about an advancing fire line too late may lose the chance to protect a transmission corridor. A hospital that receives unclear evacuation guidance may delay a hard decision. A field crew that misses an update may move toward danger instead of away from it. Information must reach the right people immediately, wherever they are, on a device they can access.


## Wildfire Detection Technology Solves Half the Problem


Governments and emergency services are investing in earlier detection, improved mapping, and stronger information sharing. AI can help identify ignitions sooner. Drones can support perimeter mapping and damage assessment. Predictive models can estimate spread based on wind, terrain, and fuel conditions. Satellite data and shared operational systems can help organizations coordinate with better situational awareness.


Wildfires increasingly affect critical infrastructure, including energy networks, water systems, transportation corridors, telecommunications, healthcare services, and public safety operations. As a result, effective response depends on more than emergency services alone. It requires coordinated action across both public- and private-sector organizations.


These tools can generate valuable intelligence. They do not, by themselves, tell a fire chief which crews to move, alert a utility control room, notify a school district, or reach residents in a threatened evacuation zone.


That is the operational gap leaders need to address. The question is not only which detection system to buy. It is whether the organization is ready to act on the intelligence that system provides:


-


*How are evacuation decisions communicated to affected residents, and through how many channels?*


-


*How are field personnel notified when conditions change mid-shift?*


-


*How are infrastructure operators, including electric utilities and water systems, alerted when a fire threatens their assets?*


-


*How are executives and decision-makers kept informed as a situation evolves over hours or days?*


-


*How do multiple agencies, often with no shared communication system, coordinate during rapidly changing conditions?*


If the answer still depends on a phone call, an email, or a person manually forwarding an alert, the organization may have improved detection without improving response.


## Wildfire Response Is Fundamentally a Communications Challenge


Once a fire is detected, the challenge changes. The priority becomes moving verified information across teams, agencies, infrastructure operators, and affected communities fast enough to support decisions under pressure.


This is more than traditional mass notification.


A wildfire incident may require one message for a lineworker, another for a utility operations center, another for a school superintendent, and another for an emergency management agency, all within minutes. Broad alerts have a role, but targeted communication is what turns warning into coordinated action.


Operational resilience depends on moving information without relying on one fragile channel, one overwhelmed call center, or one person to relay updates. BlackBerry® AtHoc® supports this coordination by bringing alerting, personnel accountability, and two-way communication into a single workflow. The goal is straightforward: make sure intelligence from detection systems reaches the people who need to act, in the format and channel they are most likely to use.


## Preparing for the Next Wildfire Season


Agencies and organizations should treat wildfire modernization as an execution challenge. Investment in detection, modeling, mapping, and inter-agency coordination can improve readiness only when it is matched by communication workflows that move at incident speed. The work cannot wait for the next major fire to expose gaps in how information moves.


-


**Connect detection systems to notification workflows.** A fire detection alert that requires manual relay to an operations center has already lost minutes an organization cannot recover.


-


**Establish pre-defined emergency response plans.** Decide, before a fire starts, who gets notified, in what order, and through what channel.


-


**Create stakeholder communication groups before an event occurs.** Utility operators, school districts, and neighboring jurisdictions should already be in a shared communication structure before the first ignition is detected.


-


**Conduct regular exercises and simulations.** A communication plan that has not been tested under time pressure is a plan with unknown failure points.


-


**Ensure multi-channel communication capabilities.** Field personnel and residents do not all monitor the same channel. Redundancy across SMS, voice, mobile app, and desktop alerting matters when infrastructure is strained.


-


**Enable coordination across public- and private- sector partners.** Utilities, transportation authorities, and private infrastructure operators need a seat in the same communication structure as government responders, not a separate one.


## Detection Creates the Opportunity, Communication Delivers the Outcome


Wildfire technology will keep improving. Detection will get earlier, modeling will get sharper, and data will move faster. Those gains matter, but they only become meaningful when organizations can convert them into timely decisions, coordinated action, and clear communication.


The organizations best prepared for the next wildfire will not be defined only by how quickly they detect a threat. They will be defined by how quickly they reach the people who need to know, align the organizations that need to respond, and keep information moving as conditions change. Early warning creates the opportunity. Communication turns that opportunity into resilience.
